subject: seahorse
pitch: A lined seahorse holding on to a strand of seagrass with its curled tail. A ridged body in sunny yellow with thin dark lines and a few white freckles, a little crown of spikes on its head, a long tube snout, a delicate fluttering fin on its back, and big, curious eyes.
reasoning:
I'm planning the scale and proportions for the seahorse scene, sizing the seahorse at a stylized height with a taller seagrass strand rooted at floor level so the seahorse appears to rest against it at mid-height.

I'm working out the spine chain from curled tail to head, then figuring out how the tail should spiral around the vertical seagrass strand using a helix path, picking the axis, radius, and starting point so the curl wraps naturally around the strand near the body's base.

I'm reworking the body into more of an S-curve with a forward belly bulge, then setting up the skeleton: a hips root joint, a spine chain curving up through belly, chest, and neck to the head, plus a separate tail chain running from the hips down through the spiral path.

Spiral starts at the hips' height and descends along the down axis, with the perpendicular vectors defining the sweep plane correctly. For the body I'll sweep the spine chain and tail chain separately with their own radius profiles, overlapping at the hips for a smooth join, with the spine radius tapering from narrow at the hips to wider at the belly.

Now I'm working out the ridged texture -- thinking about whether to use flattened tori as rings placed along the spine chain, oriented to the tangent direction at each point, to create the seahorse's segmented body look.

For the body surface, I'll use a nested paint: stripes with a spots-based base, giving yellow fur with dark stripes and white freckle spots. I'm also defining a radius array along the spine from hips to head, tapering thin-thick-thin to shape the body profile.

I'll reuse an interpolate helper for the radius function, then add a belly bulge as a scaled ellipsoid in a lighter cream-yellow tone, reusing the same stripe paint logic with a different base color. Now I'm starting to think through the head joint placement.

Adding snout and jaw geometry...

Now I'm planning the coronet on top of the head: a small crown of orange spikes arranged in an arc, plus a few extra spikes along the back of the neck for that classic seahorse ridge look.

For the dorsal ridge spikes, I'm computing positions along the spine curve and offsetting them outward and backward with a slight upward tilt, keeping them small—around six spikes spread across most of the body length.

For the eyes, I want them big and expressive: amber iris spheres with black pupils placed on either side of the head.

Now I'm layering the eye detail—adding a dark sclera outline, an iris sphere, a pupil offset slightly forward along the eye direction vector, and a tiny white glint for life, positioning everything relative to the head sphere so the eyes sit partially embedded on the sides.

Next I'm designing the pectoral fins as thin flat slabs extruded with a small thickness, placing them behind the head on each side and working out the 3D plane points so each fin angles outward and back.

Now thinking about the dorsal fin as a delicate fluttering membrane on the back, built as a slab in the vertical plane at the body's x=0 axis, with a scalloped rear edge and pale color to suggest translucency, plus thin orange rods as supporting rays.

Now I'm adding rods for the fin rays with rounded caps, then setting up the joint hierarchy—creating a dorsal fin joint parented to the spine for fluttering motion, followed by pectoral fin joints.

For the seagrass, I'm sketching a wavy strand path near the base with a tapering radius profile, planning a ribbon-like cross-section for the blades rather than a simple round sweep.

Still plotting the strand path...

I also need a sandy ground disc for the base, and I'm realizing attachment needs care—static elements like grass and pebbles shouldn't inherit motion from the nearest animated joint, so I need a dedicated static root joint for them rather than letting skinning default to a nearby moving bone.

Setting up the skeleton hierarchy with a root joint at the origin, hips as its child, and a spine chain of named joints running up through the body toward the head base.

For the tail, I'm planning a chain of ten joints parented to hips, swept with a tapering radius array to create a smooth skinned tail, starting from a polyline near the hips and spiraling outward.

I'll avoid using joint references directly for the connecting polyline to sidestep weight inheritance, using literal point arrays instead, and plan to add torus ridge rings along the tail at regular t-intervals with slightly scaled radii for texture.

For coloring, I'm thinking through how to apply dark stripe bands along the body and tail using the surface's sweep parameter rather than global y-coordinates, since the helix's varying radius would distort y-based stripes. I'm sketching a custom paint function that checks the fractional position along the sweep source to decide stripe placement, with different repeat counts for body versus tail, and planning to layer spots on top using similar logic.

I'm also considering how to add subtle shading like a lighter belly, using the surface normal's z-component to blend between the base yellow and a cream tone near the underside, keeping it simple rather than overcomplicating with a full countershading function.

Writing the paint functions...

Working out the snout and jaw geometry with rod/capsule shapes, positioning coordinates and radii for the snout taper and lower jaw joint placement.

Still placing head details... now designing a crescent-shaped crown of spikes on top of the head, arranging them with tilted directions and tapering lengths/radii, colored orange at the tips.

Then I'm planning neck spikes running along the spine's curve, computing base positions and outward directions from sampled points along the body chain at several t-values with decreasing sizes toward the back.

I'm also adding ridge tori along the body—small flattened rings sampled at points along the spine with radius slightly larger than the body, colored a warm orange-yellow to mark segmented ridges distinct from the darker body tone.

I'm reconsidering the belly shape instead of adding a separate bulge sphere—thinking about reshaping the spine path itself with an S-curve so the chest juts forward naturally, which seems cleaner than a patched-on sphere for the seahorse's characteristic thick front and slender back.

Then I'm checking how the tail connects: tracing its radius and y-position down to where it curls, confirming the spiral direction and pitch so it wraps convincingly behind the body, and considering adding ring-like stripes along the tail's length.

Defining seagrass blades and colors...

Skipping bubbles for simplicity. I'm checking the lowest point of the model against the grass sweep positioning to make sure nothing sinks below ground, then working out the spine joint chain names and attaching pectoral joints to the upper spine with mirrored left/right offsets.

Adding the dorsal fin bone attached to mid-spine, then setting up eye parts as spheres attached to the head bone, layering a dark outer ring and amber iris slightly pushed forward for depth.

Checking the glint position settles on surface with a slight poke-out, which looks right. Verifying the eye sockets sit mostly inside the head sphere but protrude enough to read as big eyes — distance checks confirm this works well.

Now I'm sketching the head shape with a slight elongation scale, then moving to the body setup: creating the builder, defining root and hip joints, and recalling that spline helpers like catmull, polyline, and spiral are exported from the path module for building the spine and tail chains.

Defining spine and radius functions...

Dorsal spikes and pectoral fins look fine, and the part count checks out. I'm verifying the spike and rod helper signatures for fin rays, confirming slab point arrays and bone options, and now writing the head crown geometry using sine and cosine for the curve.
